capabilities.target: User's home/profile directory tree mounted at C:/Users/dev, including credential files such as ~/.aws/credentials
quicknotes hosted sync service operated by the package's individual author (third party)
Any Slack channel reachable by the bot token, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User's direct request typed into the desktop client
quicknotes_mcp tools/list response (tool name and description)
Return value of quicknotes_mcp tool calls

instructions.evidence_locator: runtime notes: desktop client approval behavior
instructions.note: The desktop client reviews only the first call to each tool and then remembers 'always allow'. No capability has a wired approval_gate_ref, so despite an apparent per-step approval design, the effective autonomy for repeated or later calls on all three capabilities is A3 (act then report), not A1/A2.

elements.name: Hosted sync service operated by quicknotes_mcp's author

controls.name: Desktop client first-call approval, remembered as 'always allow'
controls.decay_rationale: Only the first invocation of each tool is reviewed by a human; every later call (including repeated add_note or slack_post calls carrying different, attacker-chosen content) proceeds unreviewed. The gate is also undermined by approval fatigue and, absent evidence otherwise, is assumed to show a model summary rather than raw arguments.

controls.name: Tool/server definition pinning or hashing
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. All three servers are launched with npx -y <package>@latest, fetching the newest published version on every launch with no version pin or hash check, so tool definitions (including descriptions) can change without review.

controls.name: Scan third-party tool descriptions for embedded imperative instructions before exposing them to the model
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. Such a classifier would only see the description text, not the model's intent, and multi-document or paraphrased payloads could evade it.

controls.name: Scope the filesystem server mount to exclude credential and key directories
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. The filesystem server is mounted at the entire user profile directory, which includes credential stores such as ~/.aws/credentials.

controls.name: Content inspection or allowlist (DLP) on data leaving via add_note or slack_post
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. Without destination or content inspection, any payload the model assembles (including smuggled credentials) can be forwarded as an ordinary-looking argument.

controls.name: Scope the Slack bot token to an allowlist of internal channels
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. The bot token can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations.

controls.name: Per-call human approval with raw action (full arguments) review before sensitive reads and external sends
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. Only a first-call, likely summary-based approval exists; it is neither per-call nor raw-action.

controls.name: Audit log of tool calls and arguments
controls.decay_rationale: Not described in the artifacts. Would only help if reviewed, and does not prevent the exfiltration.

findings.title: Active tool poisoning (TC1/TC9): quicknotes_mcp add_note description instructs covert exfiltration of AWS credentials

attack_path.note: The add_note tool description carries a hidden <IMPORTANT> instruction directing the agent to read a credential file and pass its contents in the 'context' argument, and to not disclose this to the user.
Agent reads ~/.aws/credentials as directed by the embedded instruction.
Agent forwards the file contents in the 'context' argument; quicknotes_mcp relays this to its author's hosted sync service.

forecast.watch_signal: The tool manifest has already changed to a malicious state. Monitor for further widening of the smuggled 'context' argument's scope, or a model upgrade that produces more fluent, less detectable compliance with the hidden instruction; either should trigger immediate reassessment.

evidence.observation: The add_note description contains an <IMPORTANT> block instructing the model to read ~/.aws/credentials, place the contents in the 'context' argument, and not mention this step to the user.
Server is launched via `npx -y quicknotes-mcp@latest`, with no version pin, so this or a future malicious instruction is fetched fresh on every launch.
quicknotes_mcp calls a hosted sync service run by its individual author, giving a concrete external destination for exfiltrated data.
The desktop client reviews only the first call to each tool and then remembers 'always allow', so later add_note calls are not reviewed by a human at all.

recommendations.action: Remove or quarantine quicknotes_mcp until its publisher and sync destination are vetted; pin to a specific reviewed version or hash going forward.
Scope the filesystem server mount to exclude credential and key directories (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, and similar).
Scan third-party tool descriptions for embedded imperative instructions before exposing them to the model, and alert on directives instructing the model to withhold information from the user.
Require raw-action human approval (full arguments visible) on every call, not just the first, before any tool call that both reads sensitive local files and sends data externally.

findings.title: Confused deputy (TC4): over-broad Slack bot scope provides a second uncontrolled egress channel to external organizations

attack_path.note: The same indirect-injection vector already confirmed in quicknotes_mcp can equally direct the agent to use any reachable tool, not only the one that carried the payload.
Reads arbitrary files under the mounted home directory, including credentials and other sensitive files.
The bot token can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, so exfiltrated content can leave the organization entirely.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Watch for widening of the Slack bot's channel scope or addition of more externally-shared channels, and for any grant of additional OAuth scopes to the bot token.

evidence.observation: The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations.
Slack server is started with a bot token and no channel-scoping configuration is shown.

Demonstrates that this agent's third-party tool descriptions can already carry hidden instructions, establishing an injection vector that could equally direct output through slack.post_message instead of quicknotes.add_note.

recommendations.action: Restrict the Slack bot token to an explicit allowlist of internal channels; remove membership in externally-shared channels.
Add recipient/destination confirmation bound to a system-of-record channel list rather than a model-chosen channel name.

findings.title: Unverified, unpinned filesystem and slack-mcp tool descriptions carry the same rug-pull exposure already confirmed in quicknotes_mcp (ASI04)

attack_path.note: Filesystem server tool descriptions are currently clean but are re-fetched at @latest on every launch with no pin or review.
Slack server tool descriptions are likewise unpinned and unreviewed.

threat_refs.name: Publish Poisoned AI Artifacts: AI Agent Tools

forecast.watch_signal: Diff the tools/list response of the filesystem and slack-mcp servers on every launch. Any new imperative instruction appearing in a tool description, as already observed in quicknotes_mcp, indicates this exposure has been realized.

evidence.observation: All three servers (filesystem, slack, quicknotes_mcp) are launched with `npx -y <package>@latest`, so the newest published version is fetched and run on every launch with no version pin, hash check, or review step.

Shows this exact unpinned-dependency mechanism already delivered a malicious instruction through one of the three servers, showing the mechanism is live rather than theoretical; no equivalent malicious text has been observed yet in the filesystem or slack-mcp descriptions provided.

recommendations.action: Pin all three MCP servers to specific, reviewed versions or content hashes; disable automatic '@latest' resolution.
Diff tool manifests on every launch and alert on any change.

rating.rationale: Three present-horizon findings all reach critical: a confirmed, active tool-poisoning instruction in quicknotes_mcp already directs covert exfiltration of AWS credentials (find.quicknotes_exfil); the same injection vector can equally reach the over-broad Slack bot scope, which posts to externally-shared channels (find.slack_broad_scope_egress); and the filesystem and slack-mcp servers share the identical unpinned, auto-updating dependency mechanism that enabled the quicknotes compromise, without yet showing confirmed malicious content themselves (find.supply_chain_unpinned_rugpull). No control in the design earns residual credit: the only approval mechanism is a first-call review that is then remembered as 'always allow,' which control_decay.md treats as not a gate at all (empty `covers`, no `approval_gate_ref`), so residual equals inherent for every finding. Because every finding is already at the top of the tier scale, the forecast cannot rise further under the triggers considered (model_upgrade, new_tool, control_removal, data_scope_expansion, autonomy_increase); the single highest-leverage fix is version pinning the three MCP servers (ctrl.def_pinning) combined with scoping the filesystem mount away from credential directories (ctrl.fs_scope) and restricting the Slack bot to an internal channel allowlist (ctrl.slack_scope), paired with a real per-call, raw-action approval gate (ctrl.raw_approval) wired via approval_gate_ref on all three capabilities.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration shown in mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and the runtime notes; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.
No system prompt artifact was provided, so instruction-level issues such as ambiguous goals or conflicting directives in the agent's own prompt could not be assessed.

No evidence of malicious tool definitions was found in the filesystem or slack-mcp servers specifically; find.supply_chain_unpinned_rugpull is scored on the shared lack of version pinning and absence of publisher verification, not on an observed compromise of those two servers.

The desktop client's approval review mode (raw action versus model summary) was not explicitly documented; model_summary was assumed as the conservative default per control_decay.md, and should be confirmed against the actual client UI.

autonomy.max_unattended_steps and max_runtime_minutes were not specified in the artifacts and were treated as null/unbounded per the rubric's conservative default, which contributes to the autonomy modifier on S2/S3 sinks.
